notes.key_messages: • When plotting graphs, points should be plotted as a cross ( x ) or an encircled dot (  ) and not just a small dot which is obscured by the graph line, which should be drawn using a sharp pencil. A line of best fit can be curved or straight – whichever i s the best fit for the data points. Straight lines should be drawn with the aid of a rule r and not drawn freehand, curves should be smooth and not just a line which moves from point to point. A best fit line should have an approximately equal number of points on each side of the line (excluding anomalous results) . Ca ndidates will need to decide if the l ine should be curved or straight; if a straight line has the points at either end of the line on one side of the line and the points in the middle on the other side, then the best - fit line should probably be a curve. Graph scales should be chosen such that the plotted data takes up over half of the available space and it is recommended that each major grid line should be equivalent to 1, 2, or 5 (or those numbers multiplied by 10 ) – this is indicated in the Presentation of Data section of the syllabus in t he section entitled ‘ Graphs ’ (and also recommended by the Association for Science Education (A.S.E.)). • Readings recorded from a given item of apparatus should all be recorded to the same resolution (the same number of decimal places). • In the qualitative analysis question ( Question 3 ) , where a question states that any gas produced is tested then candidates are expected to record the details for the gas test that gives a positive result. Candidates are expected to use the term ‘precipitate’ when describing the formation of a solid from t he reaction between two solutions; if when two solutions are mixed the product becomes cloudy and opaque then a precipitate has been formed. To state that a gas is given off is not an observation. The relev ant observation would be effervescence or fizzing or bubbles (of a gas). • When a question asks for the name of a chemical, a correct formula is normally acceptable. However, if a candidate answers with an incorrect formula, then credit will not be awarded. When a question asks candidates to identify ions or a substance then candidates may answer using names of formulae. • In qualitative analysis, not all of the tests described will necessarily give a positive result; a negative test result is useful since it tells us that a certain ion is not in the compound being tested.
notes.general_comments: The vast majority of candidates successfully attempted all of the questions and the full range of marks was seen. The vast majority of candidates were able to complete all questions in the time available. The paper discriminated successfully between candid ates of different abilities but was accessible to all. The paper was generally well answered, with very few blank spaces. S ome candidates omit ted Question 1(d) where the answer need ed to be written on a diagram and there is no dotted answer line. These errors of omission would not occur if candidates read the whole of the questions on the examination paper rather than just looking for dotted lines on which answers should be written. In answering the planning question ( Question 4 ) , there is no need for candidates to write a list of apparatus at the start, nor the aims of the experiment, nor a list of safety precautions or a list of dependent and independent variables. Where there is credit available for the use of suitable apparatus, then this will only be awarded if it is stated what the apparatus is used for . Credit will not be awarded just for a name in a list of other apparatus.
notes.1a: Many candidates found this question accessible with the majority correctly identifying the conical flask and the gas syringe as the items of apparatus in the diagram. Candidates who performed less well incorrectly identified the gas syringe as a ruler or a measuring tube or measuring cylinder.
notes.1b: Candidates often did not refer to the information on the question regarding the temperature range required for fermentation. Many candidates simply said to ‘ keep it at a constant temperature ’ or ‘ to maintain the temperature ’ . Stronger responses stated that the water bath is used to keep the mixture between 25  C and 35  C. Fermentation is exothermic and without cooling it can exceed 35  C , but in a cool environment the temperature can cool to below 25  C .
notes.1c: This was well answered with most candidate s correctly stat ing that the volume of gas was still increasing or that it had not stopped making gas.
notes.1d: Most candidates were able to draw two arrows to show where heat was needed, under the mineral wool and under the magnesium ribbon. A significant number drew no arrows, presumably because there was no dotted answer line and they did n o t see or read the question. A few drew arrows to the rubber tubing.
notes.1e: While the majority of candidates correctly stated that distillation should be used, a significant number of candidates incorrectly stated filtration.
notes.1f: F ewer than half correctly realise d that there is air in the apparatus at the beginning of the experiment. Some candidates mentioned steam, although this would have condensed.
notes.2a: Candidates performed well on this question and the most gained full credit . The most common errors included incorrect readings from the diagrams and leaving times in minutes and seconds rather than converting to seconds only. Almost all candidates had recorded the times to the nearest whole number. It is generally not appropriate to quote reaction times in tenths or hundredths of a second for chemistry experiments due to factors like limitations in measurement precision.
notes.2b: Most of the graphs had a suitable scale on the y - axis, usually 2 cm grid square = 10 seconds. Some candidates selected difficult scales where each 2 cm grid square was 1.5 or 3; these candidates often made errors in plotting. Each large grid square should be 1, 2 or 5  10 . The points were generally correctly plotted. There were many who thought that lines of best fit must be straight lines. The curves of best fit were often poorly drawn. S traight sections on a curve of best fit, very thick lines or any double line where a gap is visible between the lines not acceptable.
notes.2c: Most candidates were able to continue their graph line to the right so that a reading could be made at 45 cm . A significant number of candidates did not include the unit (  C) in their answer; all physical quantities should be accompanied by a unit.
notes.2d: The calculation of the energy given out was completed successfully by the majority of candidates. A few incorrectly rounded 850.5 to 850.
notes.2e: Most candidates realised that the increased mass of anhydrous lithium chloride would result in an increased temperature change. However, to gain full credit candidates were required to give a quantitative answer. Two different quantitative answer were accepted: • The temperature change would be double the temperature change of Experiment 1 because the mass of anhydrous lithium chloride had doubled. • The temperature change would be the same as Experiment 4 because the ratio of anhydrous lithium chloride : water was the same as in Experiment 4. Some candidates incorrectly based their explanation on more anhydrous lithium chloride requiring more energy to dissolve. As the process is exothermic, energy is released and not taken in.
notes.2f: This was found to be the most challenging question on the paper and few correct answers were seen. Many candidates incorrectly related their answer to surface area and rate of reaction without realising that a beaker will have a larger cross section and so result in a shallower depth of liquid; t his makes it easier to see through and so it takes more time for the text to be obscured.
notes.2gi: The vast majority of candidates correctly stated that a burette measures volumes more accurately than a measuring cylinder.
notes.2gii: This proved to be a demanding question. In the experiments , heat energy is given out and results in the temperature of the solution increasing. Heat energy lost from the system (the beaker) results in a smaller temperature increase. If the beaker is stood in a water - bath then more heat energy will be transferred f rom the beaker to the water - bath and so the temperature change will be even smaller, or possibly so small as to be not measurable with the apparatus provided. Water - baths maintain a constant temperature and so are not suitable when the dependent variable (the required outcome of the investigation) is the temperature change.
notes.3a: As the question stated that NaOH should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is form ed on dropwise addition which should dissolve in excess.
notes.3b: Similarly, as the question stated that aqueous ammonia should be added dropwise and then in excess, candidates should give an observation for each step. As solution L contained an aluminium salt, a white precipitate is form ed on dropwise addition which should remain excess. Candidates who made use of the notes for qualitative analysis on the last two pages of the question paper normally performed well on Questions 3(a) and 3(b).
notes.3c: Again, candidates who made use of the notes for qualitative analysis on the last two pages of the question paper normally stated correctly that a white precipitate would form as solution L contained chloride ions.
notes.3e: This was an accessible question for candidates and most could identify the gas given off from the nitrate test as ammonia.
notes.3f: Candidates who performed well often gained full credit for the identification of solid M as barium nitrate. It was not uncommon for candidates to identify only that solid M contained barium ions and not include an anion in their answer.
notes.3g: Many candidates correctly identified solid K as potassium nitrate. It was not uncommon for candidates to identify just one of the ions, normally the potassium ion from the flame test colour.
notes.1di: Candidates found this question easy and most candidates could state the effect of carbon dioxide on limewater was for the limewater to turn cloudy. Candidates who performed well were able to state that the cloudiness observed was due to the formation of a white precipitate.
notes.1dii: This question proved to be more demanding. Stronger responses from candidates who performed well gave the expected answer that there would be no more bubbles (because no more gas would be made ) . Weaker responses stated that the limewater would stop turning cloudy or changing, but if it is already cloudy you cannot see if it stops turning cloudy.
notes.2ci: Candidates performed well on this question and were able to calculate the relative rate using the formula given. Candidates who did not evaluate the fraction gained no credit as there had been no attempt at a calculation.
notes.2cii: This was one of the most accessible questions on the paper and almost all candidates identif ied that experiment 1 had the greatest relative rate.
notes.2di: Most candidates were able to calculate the volume of water and give the appropriate unit. Less well performing candidates found this question difficult , as they had not understood that the total volume of solution had to remain constant. They often gained credit for units even with an incorrect calculation. ( ii) Nearly all candidates could work out the relevant time for the text to not be visible at 37 cm . To gain full credit working had to be shown as stated in the question . The clearest working is the use of construction lines. Candidates who performed less well chose the incorrect volume; the most 3 3 common was using 36 or 38.5 cm rather than 37 cm .
notes.2diii: Candidates performed poorly on this question and found it very challenging. Most candidates just restated ‘so that the total volume is kept constant’ or said ‘ so that it is a fair test ’ . Few appreciated that if the total volume changes between experiments, you are introducing a second variable, which would make it unclear whether any changes in reaction rate are due to concentration or to volume.
notes.2ei: This was the most accessible question on the paper , with almost all candidates having an understanding that burettes measure volumes more accurately than measuring cylinders.
notes.2eii: This question was answered well. Candidates were able to state that either pipettes had fixed volumes or that the pipette sizes available were too small and could not hold the larger variable volumes of sodium thiosulfate required.
notes.3d: The test carried out was the test for sulfate ions. As solid L was a chloride there should have been no change. A common error was to say a white precipitate would form (the positive result in the sulfate test). It is important that the candidates use all the information given to them in the question.
